extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of medieval natural philosophy and theology (Latin scholastic readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains causal criteria used in a medieval Latin natural-philosophical/theological treatise for (a) the nature and perfection of intellects/angels and (b) meteorological phenomena (rain, snow, hail, thunder, floods, lakes, winds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beatitude/ felicity of souls and intellections
rubrics_metrics.description: Beatitude consists in secure, perpetual rest and freedom from pain and disturbance; the dead in the Lord are called blessed because they possess perfect tranquility and are free from the annoyances of bodily life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts mortal life (full of fear, suspicion, company) with the serene rest of the blessed dead: beatitude is characterized by eternal quietude, freedom from suffering and perturbation, and possession of an immutable good. Explanatory remarks emphasize that felicity is incompatible with change and diminution; infinite felicity belongs only to God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees and orders of intelligences / angels
rubrics_metrics.description: Angelic hierarchies are ordered groups (e.g., angelic sarchies, thrones, dominations, virtues, principates, powers, cherubim, seraphim) differing in proximity to God and in their capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise lists named orders and stresses that each order differs more from another than human ranks differ among themselves; none lack any perfection but differ by genus. It notes that our human intellect is only a shadow or image of the true intellects and cannot fully comprehend the divine brightness; the number of intelligences is not simply small and their full extent is beyond human reckoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of an intellect (criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect intellect is clear, certain, constant, perpetually active, and able to know by demonstration; demonstration and continuous, unmixed operation are marks of perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts our intellect (obscure, doubtful, receiving from sensible images) with a higher intellect that is clear and continuous. Demonstrative knowledge and completeness (no lack in cognition) are given as signs of perfection: an intellect that attains demonstration and order (like numbers producing cubes) is more perfect than one that only has shadowy, partial knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celestial intelligences as causes of terrestrial virtues (planetary correspondences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Celestial bodies govern elements and living things; each planet has associated intelligences/princes and virtues that produce characteristic effects on bodies and souls (e.g., Moon/Gabriel governs moisture and life; Mercury/Raphael governs senses and intellect; Venus/Anael governs fertility and delight; Sun/Michael confers strength; Mars grants boldness; Saturn firmness and longevity; Jupiter moderation and prosperity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text names specific princes and links them to functions: Gabriel with the Moon and nourishing strength, Raphael with Mercury and medicine, Anael with Venus and procreation, Michael with the Sun and firm life, Samael with Mars and potency, Sachiel with Jupiter and moderation/quies, Cassiel with Saturn and hope/long duration, etc. It emphasizes that virtues flow from higher intelligences through planetary order to earthly effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary conditions for rain (pluvia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rain requires humid vapor to remain and congregate rather than be dissipated by the sun; many vapors must gather and be condensed into clouds and then descend as rain. If vapor is dissipated by solar heat, rain will not occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seasonality and the sun's position matter: when the sun's heat is moderate (e.g., certain seasons or latitudes), vapor can accumulate and be condensed; in torrid zones the sun often dissipates vapors preventing rain. Local factors (proximity of mountains, seas, lakes, and inward/outward airflow) and duration of solar presence determine humidity and hence rains. The treatise explains why rains are more likely when the sun is not too strong or when vapors are trapped and cannot diffuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction and generation of snow, frost (pruina), and hail (grandine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Snow, frost, and hail arise from different behaviors of vapors and cold: snow is formed from higher, thinner vapors that freeze as they ascend; frost (pruina) forms from denser, earthy vapors near houses/walls; hail requires compression/coagulation of vapor into ice (and often wind-driven compression) so that it forms solid ice, sometimes large as stones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text details altitude and vapor-thickness effects: higher, tenuous vapors freeze differently than lower, dense vapors; hail needs a compressive action (not merely cold) and usually forms where vapors are compressed into ice (e.g., by certain cloud dynamics). Snow and hail often accompany particular wind and seasonal configurations; frost tends to appear near structures where vapors condense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of thunder and lightning (tonitrua et fulgur)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thunder and lightning arise when dense clouds are ruptured and sulphurous or ignitable parts of vapor ignite or descend; ignition occurs when moist interior parts are heated or when winds and opposing movements cause friction/ignition; the densest part of a cloud gives first impulse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise associates lightning with ignition of sulphurous material in lower parts of clouds, and thunder with the sudden rupture and rapid motion of cloud parts; it also notes that sometimes lightning ascends if upper parts are rarer and the impulse is upward. Winds and contrasts between denser and rarer cloud layers contribute to the phenomenon. Cases where snow falls without lightning are explained by insufficient ascent of terrestrial sulphurous vapors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of winds and their direction in storms and ship safety
rubrics_metrics.description: The danger to a ship depends on the wind's relation to the ship's heading: winds from ahead or obliquely can cause greater peril and submergence, whereas a wind following (aft) is safer; combinations of winds (contrary directions) and strong upward or downward gusts cause larger perturbations and inundations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives practical rules: if a single wind blows squarely along the river or sea, less flooding occurs than if oblique winds drive water against banks. Opposing winds (contrary currents) can overwhelm a vessel; sailing with a following (aft) wind is safer. The magnitude of storm effects scales with the size of the water body: sea > lake > river.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of inundations and river floods (e.g., the Nile)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inundations result from multiple causes: heavy rains feeding rivers, wind-driven transfer of water, accumulation/compression of sources (springs, lakes), and seasonal solar positions that alter evaporation and condensation patterns; the Nile’s annual flood is attributed to seasonal rains and the gathering of vapors in the regions where its sources lie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise explains that flood magnitude depends on the quantity of water, the strength/direction of winds, and the geography of basins and outlets. It uses the Nile as example: rains in distant regions, the timing of the sun's path, and compression of upstream sources can cause the Nile to swell and flood Egyptian plains. The text also mentions that lake and sea interactions and the temporary constriction of outlets produce periodic rises and falls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation, maintenance, and differences among lakes, seas, and marshes
rubrics_metrics.description: A lake requires a basin bounded by mountains or hills, an inlet of sufficient inflow and an outlet (or a lower rim) so water is not entirely dispersed; if inflow ceases or outflow is blocked, a lake can become a marsh or evaporate into a dry basin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise lists conditions for persistent lakes: collection of water by surrounding topography, a lower outlet to prevent complete overflow, and sufficient inflow. It distinguishes lakes from seas and marshes by permanence and circulation: lakes that regularly dry are actually marshes, while a lake needs movement and depth to remain a lake rather than a stagnant pool.
